learning_objectives.9.1: Explain why a regulation matters only insofar as it changes behavior — working through entrepreneurs and the production structure.
learning_objectives.9.2: Explain why the 'seen' before-and-after effect of a regulation misleads, because the market is a process, not a controlled experiment.
learning_objectives.9.3: Explain why judging a regulation requires the 'unseen' counterfactual — the foregone alternative is its real cost (the minimum-wage worker who is laid off).
learning_objectives.9.4: Explain what the 'unrealized' is — the future value a regulation forecloses (the trainee's lost career and lost future output) — and why, over time, it is the largest and truest cost.
learning_objectives.9.5: Given a novel regulation, determine its seen, unseen, and unrealized effects.

Chapter 9 → Regulatory Intervention.text: Regulations are government restrictions — prohibitions, licenses, standards, price controls, quotas, subsidies — all intended to induce change in the economy. They matter only if and to the extent they change behavior; an inapplicable or unenforced rule changes nothing. Because the production structure is determined by entrepreneurs pursuing profit from consumer wants, effective regulation works by changing which production projects entrepreneurs undertake — whether it targets producers directly or reaches them through changed consumer demand.

Chapter 9 → The Seen.text: The observable world is the obvious starting point for judging a regulation — and a misleading one. The market is a process in constant flux, so a regulation is never the only change: before-and-after comparisons cannot isolate its effect. After a $14 minimum wage, the example employer's average wage rises from $11 to $15 — an apparent success. But the average rose partly because the lowest-paid worker, the trainee, was let go.

Chapter 9 → The Unseen.text: The unseen is the other side of the story: what would otherwise have happened. It cannot be measured — only reasoned out — yet it is the cost of any choice; the value of the foregone alternative. Counting only the seen makes analysis one-sided: benefit with no cost. A minimum wage does not raise wages; it forbids employing anyone below the floor. In the counterfactual, all three workers stay employed, and the trainee's wage rises with his productivity.

Chapter 9 → The Unrealized.text: The market is a process, so today's world shapes the future. Beyond the unseen lies the unrealized: the future value the regulation forecloses. The laid-off trainee loses not just a job but the experience that would have raised his productivity — his career. His lost output, and the demand his earnings would have funded, never come to be. The economy sits on a lower-value trajectory; the unrealized is the true cost of regulations, and it far exceeds the unseen.

items.stem: What three-part tool does the chapter offer for analyzing any regulation?
options: Intent, text, and enforcement
Costs, benefits, and externalities
The seen, the unseen, and the unrealized
Supply, demand, and equilibrium

items.stem: True or false: per the chapter, economics can identify a regulation's full results but cannot decide whether it was 'worth it' — that is a value judgment.
options: True
False

items.stem: Why must a regulation's unseen be constructed by reasoning rather than measured?
options: Statistical methods remain too primitive
Governments conceal the relevant records
Business surveys are notoriously unreliable
What never happened leaves no data; logic must reach it

items.stem: A city's report on its new food-truck licensing fee lists: fees collected, trucks licensed, and inspections passed. In the chapter's terms, what kind of accounting is this?
options: An unrealized analysis of the program's future
An unseen analysis, since fees are invisible to diners
A complete cost-benefit analysis
Seen-only — the one-sided view

items.stem: Ridgeway requires every new rental apartment to include a parking space. Five years on, officials report success: 12,000 compliant units built, low vacancy, and rents up — attributed to 'higher-quality housing stock.' Applying the chapter's framework, which of the following is the regulation's UNSEEN?
options: The cheaper, garage-free apartments that never went up
The enforcement costs the city has not publicized
Repair bills the mandated garages have not yet brought
Fines the city never issued, since builders complied

items.stem: Ridgeway's parking mandate turns twenty. A retrospective tallies two decades of higher rents paid and garages maintained. Applying the chapter's framework, which cost is the regulation's UNREALIZED?
options: The households and ventures that never took root there
The fines the city never collected from compliant landlords
The parking fees tenants never had to pay separately
The rent control the council never imposed

items.stem: A city imposes a $5,000 annual license on food trucks, with inspections to enforce it. Reasoning with the chapter's full framework, where will this regulation's LARGEST cost eventually lie?
options: In the fees that operating trucks never recoup from customers
In the paperwork hours truck owners lose each year
In the city's growing enforcement budget
In the food businesses and careers that never begin

source.title: A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles

learning_objectives.1.1: Explain why the same people repeatedly line up on opposite sides of issues that have no intrinsic connection — they reason from different, usually implicit, premises about how the world works — and why the pattern is neither coincidence nor a plot.
learning_objectives.1.2: Distinguish a vision in Sowell's sense — a pre-analytic sense of causation, a hunch about how the world works that comes before any theory or test — from a dream, a hope, a prophecy, or a moral imperative.
learning_objectives.1.3: Explain why visions are indispensable yet dangerous: reality is too complex for any mind, so a vision, like a map, must leave features out — and what it leaves out may not be negligible, which is why a vision must be tested against evidence rather than mistaken for reality.
learning_objectives.1.4: Explain how vision, theory, and evidence relate — logic works a vision's consequences into a theory, and facts then discriminate between competing theories, able to refute a theory but never to prove it correct.
learning_objectives.1.5: Explain why visions shape action and history even when never articulated and even when their holders are unaware of them — filling the gaps in individual knowledge, setting the agenda, and carried by people pursuing narrower purposes.

Chapter 1 → The Role of Visions.text: A vision here is a pre-analytic sense of how causation works — closer to a hunch than to logic, and not a dream, hope, prophecy or moral imperative. Because reality is too complex to hold whole, every vision omits, so it must be tested rather than mistaken for reality. Logic builds it into theory and facts then discriminate between theories, refuting but never confirming. Visions shape action even unarticulated, filling gaps where their holders have not tested what they assume.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what provides the consistency behind the same people repeatedly opposing each other on numerous unrelated issues?
options: The issues share a hidden connection that determines every position
They reason from different premises about how the world works
So many issues arise that repeated opposition is bound to occur by chance
They belong to groups that coordinate positions in advance

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, the differing premises that keep the same people on opposite sides of unrelated issues are often implicit rather than spelled out.
options: True
False

items.stem: Why does the chapter reject both coincidence and a plot as explanations for the same people repeatedly lining up on opposite sides of unrelated issues?
options: It is really driven by special interests and personality clashes, which explain the line-up better than either would
It is out in the open, since both sides state the premises they reason from, so there is nothing to hide
It recurs too regularly for chance, yet no one controls it; it flows from the premises each side reasons from
It reflects party discipline, since organized sides vote together by rule rather than by accident or design

items.stem: The chapter says the two sides in these recurring disputes are reasoning from different premises. Premises about what?
options: About how the world works: what causes what
About which outcomes are morally required of us
About which of the disputed facts are true
About whose material interests are at stake in each case

items.stem: Why does it matter to the chapter's argument that the issues involved, from military spending and drug laws to monetary policy and education, have no intrinsic connection with one another?
options: If nothing in the issues links them, positions must rest on temperament and emotion rather than on any reasoning
If nothing in the issues links them, each side must be judging every issue on its own merits, independently of the rest
If nothing in the issues links them, the consistent line-up must come from premises the sides carry into every issue
If nothing in the issues links them, the disputes must really be about one underlying issue the others stand in for

items.stem: As the chapter uses the term, which of the following best describes a 'vision'?
options: A sense of how the world works — of what causes what — that a person holds before any theory is built or tested
A firmly held conviction about what people and their governments ought to do, stated as a guiding principle
A confident forecast of where events are heading, made before the evidence that could confirm or refute it is available
An inspiring picture of the future that a person or a movement has committed itself to bringing about

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, a person's vision typically forms after the relevant facts have been gathered and reasoned through, as the conclusion those facts point to.
options: True
False

items.stem: Which of the following statements expresses a vision in the chapter's sense — rather than a dream or hope, a prophecy, or a moral imperative?
options: If only no one ever had to fear walking home at night in their own neighborhood
Society ought to treat every offender humanely, whatever the cost to public safety
Within a generation, our cities will be safer than they have ever been before
People commit fewer crimes when they see that wrongdoing is reliably punished

items.stem: The chapter says a vision is not a dream, a hope, a prophecy, or a moral imperative — and then adds that any of these may ultimately derive from a vision. Which statement best explains how those two claims fit together?
options: A vision is a picture of what causes what; what a person then hopes for, predicts, or demands can follow from that picture, so those are its products rather than the vision itself
A vision is a hope or forecast that the facts have since borne out; the chapter's point is that a dream, hope, prophecy, or demand is simply a vision that has not yet been confirmed
A vision is whichever of those four a person holds most firmly; the chapter's point is that a hope or a moral demand, once held strongly enough, becomes a vision in its own right
A vision is the sum of a person's dreams, hopes, prophecies, and moral demands; the chapter separates them only for convenience and in practice treats the whole bundle as one vision

items.stem: A movement's founding statement reads: 'We see a country in which no family goes hungry.' In the chapter's terms, why is this statement not, by itself, the movement's vision?
options: It rests on feeling rather than on reasoning, whereas the chapter treats a vision as the product of systematic logic applied to established facts
It has not yet been tested against evidence, whereas the chapter treats a vision as a picture that has already survived such a test of the facts
It names a hoped-for result without saying what brings such results about; a vision is a picture of causes, from which such a hope may derive
It is written down and stated openly, whereas the chapter reserves the term for premises that remain implicit and are never put into words

items.stem: According to the chapter, why must a vision, like a map, leave out many concrete features of reality?
options: Because its holder has not yet gathered enough facts to fill it in, and the missing features are restored as evidence comes in.
Because a vision expresses a hope for how the world ought to be, and a hope is not meant to describe every present detail of it.
Because the features it leaves out have already been shown by evidence to make no difference to the results the vision predicts.
Because reality is too complex for any mind to grasp whole, so a vision must narrow attention to a few key paths toward a goal.

items.stem: According to the chapter, whether a vision ends up simplistic depends mainly on how carefully it was constructed, so a well-built vision need not leave out anything important.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter says it would be good to be able to dispense with visions entirely and deal only with reality, but that this may be the most utopian vision of all. Why would dispensing with visions be utopian?
options: Because visions supply the hopes and moral ideals that give political action its purpose, and no one can act politically without them.
Because people act on visions they have never articulated or even noticed, so no one could ever be sure of having given theirs up.
Because facts alone can never prove any theory correct, so reality by itself could never settle which of the competing visions is right.
Because reality is too complex for any single mind to comprehend, so the proposal assumes an ability that no one actually has.

items.stem: The chapter calls visions indispensable but dangerous. Which explanation of that pairing is consistent with the chapter?
options: Indispensable because a sufficiently careful mind can grasp reality whole through them, and dangerous only when the thinker using them is careless.
Indispensable because no mind can grasp reality whole, and dangerous because what they leave out for focus may still turn out to affect results.
Indispensable because they are what facts ultimately confirm, and dangerous because a vision once confirmed tends to discourage any further inquiry.
Indispensable because they supply the goals a society strives toward, and dangerous because those goals may prove impossible to reach in practice.

items.stem: The chapter says the mind's ability to abstract, to pick out parts and treat them as the whole, is nowhere more necessary than in social visions and social theory. Which explanation is consistent with the chapter?
options: Social phenomena, unlike physical ones, cannot be tested against evidence, so a social vision has to rest on abstraction alone rather than on any body of facts.
Social visions set the agenda for thought and action and their effects spread across generations, so they must be kept simple enough for the general public to grasp.
Social visions describe how a society ought to be rather than how it works, so they need abstraction to sketch an ideal that no existing society has yet matched.
Social phenomena involve the complex, often subconscious interactions of millions of people, so a social vision must leave many important things unexplained.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does a theory relate to the vision beneath it?
options: The vision is the theory restated in plainer, less technical language, so the two differ in wording rather than in kind or in sequence.
The vision is the foundation, and the theory is the working-out of what consequences follow if causation runs as the vision conceives it.
The theory comes first as an exercise in systematic logic, and the vision is the gut feeling a thinker forms about that theory afterward.
The vision is a summary of the hard facts a theory rests on, and the theory is the logic that connects those facts into a single system.

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, a vision's subjectivity generally carries over to the theory built on it, leaving that theory's validity beyond what facts can measure.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter calls logic an essential ingredient in turning a vision into a theory, yet insists that the initial vision is what is crucial for our glimpse of insight into how the world works. Which statement best explains this division of roles?
options: A vision fits the facts more closely than any theory derived from it, so it is the vision itself, rather than the theory, that evidence ultimately confirms or refutes.
Logic can be applied only after evidence has confirmed a theory, so it arrives too late in the process to have shaped the original insight in any way.
Discovery starts from impressions a thinker cannot fully account for; logic then works out and proves what the vision implies rather than producing the insight.
A vision is itself a compressed exercise in logic, so the insight and its proof are the same act described at two different stages of the same process.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what turns a fact into evidence?
options: Its bearing on rival theories: a fact is evidence when it counts for one theory and against another, and apart from any theory it is an isolated curiosity.
Its resistance to explanation: a fact becomes evidence when none of the theories currently under consideration is able to account for it at all.
Its agreement with the observer's vision: a fact becomes evidence once it confirms the sense of causation that led someone to look for it in the first place.
Its independence from any vision: a fact is most trustworthy as evidence when it was gathered before any theory could bias which facts were selected.

items.stem: In the chapter's account, why does passing an empirical test leave a theory short of being proved correct?
options: Because facts discriminate between visions rather than between theories, so a passed test tells us something about the underlying vision but nothing about the theory that was built on it.
Because more than one vision can fit a given fact: a test shows only which theory now under consideration is most consistent with what is known, and a better-fitting one may arrive tomorrow.
Because a test can confirm only the assumptions a theory starts from, not the consequences deduced from them, and it is those deduced consequences that would have to be proved correct.

Because the facts used in any test were selected under the influence of the very vision the theory rests on, which makes every confirmation the theory receives circular rather than genuinely independent.

items.stem: In the chapter's account, a vision influences what a decision-maker does whether or not he has ever spelled it out—and even if he does not realize he holds one.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter observes that a doctor may be a conservative on medical issues and a liberal on social and political issues, or the reverse. What point is this example used to make?
options: Expert judgment in one field tends to carry over into sound judgment on unrelated questions
Where a person lacks tested knowledge, an untested vision fills the gap and guides his actions
A vision has to be tested against evidence before a person will act on it in any field
People's political positions are chosen to serve their special interests rather than their beliefs

items.stem: A city council member says she has no use for theories or big-picture ideas about society—she is too busy solving concrete problems to bother with them. How does the chapter's account bear on her claim?
options: It suggests her vision is a well-tested one: a decision-maker who has verified her premises against evidence no longer needs to think about theory
It supports her: the chapter treats day-to-day decisions as driven by interests, emotions, and personalities, with visions mattering only to intellectuals
It supports her: a vision affects action only once it has been articulated, so a decision-maker who ignores theory is guided by the facts of each case alone
It does not exempt her: she is still acting on some underlying vision of how society works, one whose ultimate basis she has never paused to examine

items.stem: A lobbyist invokes a widely shared idea about how the economy works only because it helps him win the policy fight he is being paid to win; privately he is indifferent to whether the idea is true. How does the chapter's account treat his part in that idea's influence on history?
options: He is irrelevant to it: only people who sincerely hold an idea can pass it into the enduring currents of history, and his cynicism disqualifies him
He is evidence against it: his success shows that political outcomes are decided by interests and tactics, so the idea itself is doing no real work
He is a source of it: in the chapter's account, it is political operators of his kind who originate the visions that later dominate an era
He is a carrier of the idea: whatever his motive, he helps spread it, playing a role in its history while pursuing a much narrower aim of his own

items.stem: Carefully reasoned, explicitly stated arguments turn out to have little measurable effect on any particular election or legislative vote. Why, in the chapter's account, does this not show that visions are unimportant to such decisions?
options: Because decision-makers act on the articulated arguments they have personally examined, even when they cannot cite them at the moment of the vote
Because a vision's effect comes only afterward—the vote is decided on other grounds, and the consequences reverberate for generations
Because a vision can dominate the whole atmosphere in which a decision is made, without anyone consciously weighing it as an argument
Because intellectuals deliver their reasoning to decision-makers privately, as advice behind the scenes, where its effect cannot be measured

source.title: A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles

learning_objectives.2.1: Contrast how the two visions conceive human nature: an inherent egocentricity to be worked within — moral and social benefits produced by incentives rather than changed dispositions — versus a circumstantial selfishness that a “perfectible” (continually improvable, never perfect) man can outgrow, which makes incentives unworthy expedients.
learning_objectives.2.2: Explain why the constrained vision can hope only for trade-offs — every restraint on inherent human evils carries costs of its own, so prudence is “the first of all virtues” and ideals are weighed against their cost — while the unconstrained vision seeks solutions that end the need for trade-offs and treats process costs as regrettable but not decisive.
learning_objectives.2.3: Explain why intentions are decisive in the unconstrained vision yet nearly irrelevant in the constrained one — Godwin's virtue/vice/negligence scheme has no cell for the unintended benefit at the centre of Smith's Wealth of Nations — so that one vision states its goals as desired results and the other as process characteristics.
learning_objectives.2.4: Explain why the two visions look in opposite places for causes: where evils are the default state of limited man, the constrained vision seeks the special causes of peace, wealth, and order; where man is not inherently limited, the unconstrained vision seeks the special causes of war, poverty, and crime in institutions and foolish choices.
learning_objectives.2.5: Predict, from one unfamiliar argument or policy stance, the position its holder's vision implies on a different issue — placing the stance by whether human limitations are built into its structure or treated as removable, not by how much it speaks of limits or potential.

Chapter 2 → The Nature of Man.text: One vision treats human egocentricity as a permanent fact to be worked within: benefits are produced by incentives, honour and moral principle rather than by remaking people, and what matters is how we act, not what we spontaneously feel. The other treats present selfishness as circumstantial and man as perfectible — continually improvable, with no limit anyone can specify — so contrived rewards look like unworthy expedients standing in the way of doing right because it is right.

Chapter 2 → Trade-offs Versus Solutions.text: Where human failings are inherent, every device that restrains them carries costs of its own, so nothing is available but trade-offs and prudence ranks first among virtues; ideals are weighed against what they cost, and the reformer aims at the best people can bear. Where failings are removable, a solution can end the need to trade off at all — and that prospect is what licenses transitional costs, which are regrettable without being decisive.

Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social C.text: Sorting acts into intended and unintended benefit and harm leaves one square empty — unintended benefit — and that empty square is where an entire economics sits: gains to society that formed no part of anyone's purpose. So one vision judges by intentions and names its goals as results it wants; the other judges by systemic characteristics. Each also finds the opposite thing puzzling: one hunts the causes of war and poverty, the other the causes of peace and wealth.

Chapter 2 → Summary and Implications.text: What places a thinker is not how often he speaks of human limits or of untapped potential, but whether those limits are built into the structure of his argument or treated as something institutions imposed and reform can remove. Someone may concede a limit freely and still refuse to let it constrain his conclusions. Because the starting picture of human nature shapes everything downstream, one stated position lets you predict the rest.

items.stem: In Adam Smith's example, a European who hears that an earthquake has swallowed up China soon returns to his business, though the loss of his own little finger would cost him a night's sleep. According to the chapter, what did Smith conclude about the project of changing this egocentric nature?
options: That it was the central moral task: the European's indifference showed a failure of education that a better upbringing could and should correct.
That it was possible but costly: the European's indifference was the work of artificial passions and social customs that had corrupted natural man.
That it was desirable but premature: under the current state of things, incentives would have to serve until dispositions could be reformed.
That it was vain and pointless: making the European feel the full pain of the Chinese would be perfectly useless, except to make him miserable.

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, Godwin conceded that, as things stand, people commonly prefer a lesser interest of their own to a greater interest of others.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter reports that Godwin and Condorcet held man to be 'perfectible.' According to the chapter, what did they mean by this?
options: That man can be brought to a state of actual, absolute perfection, after which no further moral improvement would be needed or possible for the species.
That man can be improved without limit, provided the right system of rewards and punishments is kept in place to reshape his existing habits over time.
That man can be improved only up to a definite ceiling, which reason can specify in advance and beyond which no progress is possible.
That man can be improved continually, coming nearer and nearer to an ideal with no limit anyone can prescribe, yet never reaching perfection.

items.stem: Smith relied on a system of moral and economic incentives to draw benefits for others out of self-centered men. According to the chapter, why did Godwin disdain such socially contrived incentives?
options: Because he held that inducements addressed to honor, nobility, and moral principle, rather than to economic self-interest, were the only ones worthy of a rational being.
Because he doubted that incentives could move existing men at all, so deeply had prejudice, artificial passion, and social custom corrupted them beyond the reach of any reward or punishment.
Because he thought incentives might have to serve for the present, but only until education had reformed dispositions far enough to make such expedients safe to discard.
Because selfishness arose from circumstances, not from our nature, so people could do right because it is right; rewards only fostered the selfishness they were meant to curb.

items.stem: The chapter says that, for Smith, people on many occasions sacrifice their own interests to the greater interests of others. According to the chapter, how did Smith reconcile this with his picture of an egocentric human nature?
options: The feeling is egocentric, but we cannot prefer ourselves so shamelessly when we act; devices such as honor and moral principle get the sacrifice made.
Nature, having loaded us with our own sorrows, also planted a love of our neighbor as ourselves, and this sentiment moves us to their relief when their need is greater.
Man can directly feel other people's needs as more important than his own, and so can act impartially even when his own interests are involved.
Egocentricity belongs only to the current state of things; as a higher sense of social duty develops in the long run, such sacrifices become a natural inclination.

items.stem: In Sowell's account of the unconstrained vision, what precisely counts as a 'solution'?
options: A remedy whose expected benefits have been carefully weighed against the full costs of bringing it about
A state in which a trade-off is no longer necessary, even if reaching it entailed costs that are now past
The best arrangement that the people can be brought to bear, given their confirmed habits and prejudices
The most immediately effective incentive available under the current state of things, whatever men's dispositions

items.stem: According to Sowell, why can the constrained vision hope for no more than 'a prudent trade-off' in dealing with evils such as war, poverty and crime?
options: Because the natural constraints of food and death set a ceiling that no social arrangement can lift, whatever human nature turns out to be
Because sufficient moral commitment to solve them has never yet been mustered, though nothing intractable stands in the way of doing so
Because the special causes of war, poverty and crime have yet to be discovered, so any remedy must remain provisional until they are found
Because whatever restrains inherent human evils has costs of its own, including other social ills that the civilizing institutions create

items.stem: A defender of legal technicalities that let some criminals escape punishment says, 'That is the price we pay for freedom.' In Sowell's reading, which vision does the remark express, and why?
options: The constrained vision, since the speaker openly concedes that freedom carries a real cost for society
The constrained vision, since the speaker accepts an imperfect legal institution rather than trying to perfect it
The unconstrained vision, since the speaker expects the technicalities to be reformed away once wiser policies prevail
The unconstrained vision, since the cost is named only to be treated as secondary to the ideal it serves

items.stem: True or false: in Sowell's account, a 'prudent reformer' who respects the people's confirmed habits and prejudices and seeks to establish 'the best that the people can bear' leans toward the unconstrained vision, since he aims to improve society rather than leave it as it is.
options: True
False

items.stem: Sowell notes that prudence — the careful weighing of trade-offs — is 'among the highest duties' in the constrained vision but 'of a lower order of importance' in the unconstrained vision. Why the difference?
options: Because moral improvement has no fixed limit in the unconstrained vision, so a solution can supersede the trade-offs that prudence weighs
Because the unconstrained vision looks to incentives rather than to judgment to steer men toward good deeds, which makes prudence redundant
Because the unconstrained vision denies that social change carries any costs, which leaves prudence nothing to weigh against the ideal
Because the unconstrained vision treats intentions as decisive, and prudence is a matter of calculating consequences rather than of meaning well

items.stem: Sowell observes that Godwin's classification of human actions left one kind of action without any category. Which kind was it, and why does Sowell single out the omission?
options: Careless harm — the category on which Smith's account of capitalists relied
Intended harm — the category Smith found in capitalists' conspiracies against the public
Unintended benefit — the category on which Smith's Wealth of Nations turned
Intended benefit — the category Smith dismissed as scarcely worth noticing
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell indicates that, within the constrained vision, what chiefly recommends a policy is the sincerity and dedication of the people who advance it.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell notes that Adam Smith characterized the capitalist's intentions as 'mean rapacity' and described capitalists as conspiring against the public whenever they met — yet Smith became the patron saint of laissez-faire capitalism. According to Sowell, why is there no contradiction?
options: For Smith, capitalists' rapacity was a regrettable cost of the process, outweighed by the prosperity laissez-faire was meant to deliver.
For Smith, the harsh portraits were rhetorical excess; his considered view was that most capitalists genuinely intended the public good.
For Smith, competition would gradually refine capitalists' dispositions until their motives came to coincide with the public good.
For Smith, social benefit came from the systemic characteristics of a competitive economy, not from the intentions of anyone within it.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell notes that, in The Wealth of Nations, economic benefits to society were largely unintended by individuals and emerged systemically from the marketplace. Which statement correctly describes how, in Sowell's account, that process connects individual self-interest to the interest of society?
options: The process gradually replaces self-centred motives with a genuine disposition to serve the needs of others directly.
The process simply adds up the separate self-interests of individuals, and their sum turns out to be the interest of society.
The process requires each individual to do things for other people; only the motivation behind those acts is self-centred.
The process brings self-interest and the social interest into identity, so that no trade-off between them remains necessary.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell says the two visions do not merely have different goals; their goals 'relate to different things.' Which statement best explains what he means?
options: The unconstrained vision sets its goals for a distant future; the constrained vision confines its goals to what the present generation can use.
The unconstrained vision seeks results for society as a whole; the constrained vision seeks results for particular individuals and particular groups.
The unconstrained vision names the results it wants; the constrained vision names the features of a process it expects to be conducive to results.
The unconstrained vision states its goals in moral terms; the constrained vision states them in economic terms, as returns weighed against costs.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: In Sowell's account, it is believers in the constrained vision — not the unconstrained — who seek the special causes of peace, wealth, and a law-abiding society.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell says the writers of The Federalist Papers were quite conscious of the vision of man underlying the Constitution's elaborate checks and balances. In his reading, what did they take such institutions to be?
options: Chains that narrow and corrupt a nature born free and innocent
Ways of trying to cope with an evil inherent in man himself
Counterweights that needlessly complicate the machine and weigh upon the people
Devices to be retired once all citizens were devoted to their country and its laws
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell writes that believers in the unconstrained vision seek the special causes of war, poverty, and crime, while believers in the constrained vision seek the special causes of peace, wealth, and a law-abiding society. Why, in his account, does the constrained vision look in that direction?
options: Because it holds that dwelling on social evils only tempts reformers toward the utopian solutions that do more harm than the evils themselves
Because it regards war, poverty, and crime as so deeply rooted in human nature that explaining them would serve no practical purpose
Because it takes those evils to follow from man's own limitations and passions, so that it is their absence which calls for explanation
Because it traces those evils to failed institutions and rulers, whose particular failures no general account of human nature can explain
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell uses the exchange between Malthus and Godwin over population to make a point about the two visions. In his account, what did the two men actually disagree about?
options: Their pictures of human nature — whether people would needlessly multiply until subsistence became hard to achieve
Their pictures of nature itself — whether the need for food is a genuine constraint or an artifact of injurious institutions
Their view of nature's bounty — whether cultivation could raise the food supply as fast as human numbers could grow
Their arithmetic — whether a geometrical increase in population was possible, or merely a rhetorical device of Malthus's
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell notes that the French Revolution gave sweeping powers, including the power of life and death, to those who spoke in the name of the people — and that when its believers were bitterly disappointed in particular leaders, they deposed and executed them and carried on much as before. In his reading, what does that response reveal about the causal logic of the unconstrained vision?
options: It accepts the revolution's bloodshed as a regrettable cost, secondary to the solution being pursued
It locates the evil in the persons who betrayed the cause, not in the system that had empowered them
It holds that no one is ever to be completely trusted with power, so power must be checked by opposing powers
It treats the passions of men as unable to conform to reason and justice without external constraint

items.stem: According to the chapter's summary, what determines whether a thinker belongs to the constrained or to the unconstrained tradition?
options: Whether the thinker holds that human nature is wholly fixed or wholly changeable
Whether the thinker's proposals defend existing institutions or seek to replace them
Whether constraints are built into the structure and operation of the theory
Whether the thinker refers more often to human limitations than to human potential

items.stem: In Sowell's account, Rousseau's claim that man is born free but is everywhere in chains expresses the unconstrained vision.
options: True
False

items.stem: Condorcet acknowledged that human intelligence has limits, yet Sowell places him among the clearest exemplars of the unconstrained vision. What, in Sowell's account, keeps that acknowledgment from making his vision a constrained one?
options: He granted that a limit exists but held that no one could say where it lies
He granted the limit for isolated individuals but denied it for the whole species
He treated the limit as a fact of external nature rather than of human nature
He referred to human potential far more often than to human limitations

items.stem: A commentator defends legal technicalities that occasionally let a guilty person go free with the words, "That is the price we pay for freedom." Sowell files this with the unconstrained vision. Which reading explains the placement?
options: The cost is acknowledged and then denied any decisive weight against the ideal
The speaker treats freedom as a fixed limit that no reform could remove
The speaker is defending existing institutions rather than seeking to change them
The speaker weighs freedom's benefits against the cost and finds them larger

items.stem: Dana runs operations for a hospital chain. Urging the board to scrap its incident-reporting scheme of points, penalties and a league table, she says: "Let's be realistic about human nature. Put people under a scoreboard and they will bury mistakes, shift blame and protect their numbers — that is exactly what our staff have learned to do. Take the scoreboard away and the candor you find in any good clinical team comes back on its own." The chain has just bought a hospital abroad, where staff hand patients over between shifts by a long-standing local custom. On whether the chain's standard handover protocol should be adjusted to that custom, which position does Dana's vision imply?
options: Adapt the protocol to the local custom
Keep the existing local custom instead
Introduce the protocol as written
Let the local staff decide

items.stem: Marta chairs a city transit board and opens every meeting by reminding colleagues that the budget is finite and that riders are not saints. Backing a plan to make every bus and train fare-free, she gives most of her memo to the downside: fares are a third of the budget, service will thin for years, two outer neighborhoods will lose their routes, and some riders will abuse a free system. She closes: "I have hidden none of this, and it is heavy. None of it is a reason to go on running a city where a person can be priced off a bus." Marta is later asked about a puzzle in the county's schools: one district has held its dropout rate near zero for a decade while every district around it has watched dropouts climb. Which line of inquiry does Marta's vision imply she would take up first?
options: Whether that district simply counts dropouts differently
Why the surrounding districts are losing students
What that district's near-zero rate is costing it elsewhere
How that district has managed to hold on to its students
